claims.text: Wear resistance and microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding are governed by the formation and evolution of a nanocrystalline surface layer.
The governing surface layer has the equiatomic composition Fe0.2Ni0.2Cr0.2Co0.2Cu0.2.
The governing surface layer consists of FCC crystals.
The governing surface layer has an average grain size of 50 nm.
The governing surface layer is 100-200 nm thick.
The nanocrystalline surface layer improves resistance to plastic deformation and abrasive wear.
The baseline coating has an average grain size of 100 nm.
Annealing at 800°C for 1 hour produces a 50% change in coating grain size relative to the baseline.
The relevant sliding regime is 500-700°C at a sliding speed of 1 m/s.
The selected temperature and speed are justified by the coating's thermal stability and typical high-temperature sliding conditions.
Formation and evolution of the nanocrystalline surface layer reduce the coefficient of friction.
Formation and evolution of the nanocrystalline surface layer increase hardness.
The reduced friction and increased hardness enhance wear resistance.
The nanocrystalline surface layer promotes grain-boundary sliding and rotation.
Grain-boundary sliding and rotation reduce microscopic deformation.
The intervention will increase wear resistance by 25%, reducing mass loss from 10 mg to 7.5 mg.
The intervention will reduce microscopic deformation by 30%, represented by a decrease in surface roughness from 5 μm to 3.5 μm.
The predictions are limited to coatings with grain sizes of 50-200 nm and coating thicknesses of 100-500 nm.
Absence of an evolving nanocrystalline surface layer during sliding falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure to reduce mass loss by at least 1.5 mg or surface roughness by at least 0.75 μm relative to baseline falsifies the hypothesis.
